title: Sunday, September 27
text:
This morning


Creating agents
The API underneath everything, and an agent with a tool list you chose.


Managing security risks
Believing it, sending data out, letting it act — and what you take back to work.

title: Sunday, September 27
text:
A chatbot produces text

It receives text and returns text. That is the entire capability.


Everything it “knows” arrived as text in the request
Everything it “does” leaves as text in the response
No files, no network, no memory between conversations

A chatbot that appears to remember you is being handed the earlier conversation again on every turn.

title: Sunday, September 27
section: An agent is a chatbot with tools
text:
An agent is a chatbot with tools


You send a request. The harness also sends a list of tools and what each one does.
The model answers with text, or with a request to use a tool.
The harness runs the tool and puts the result back into the conversation.
Repeat until the model answers with text and no tool call.


The loop in step 4 is the whole mechanism. Nothing else is added.

title: Sunday, September 27
section: What the model is actually sent
text:
What the model is actually sent
Every turn, the harness assembles one block of text:


Fixed each turn
The system prompt. The tool definitions. Any instruction files the harness decided to include.


Growing each turn
Your messages, the model’s replies, and the full output of every tool that has run so far.



A tool result is text in the conversation, which is why a document the agent read can change what it does next.

title: Sunday, September 27
text: The API

title: Sunday, September 27
text:
A fourth door



Door
Who is at the keyboard
What it is for




Chat in a browser
you
one question


Claude Code
you
work on a machine


A connector
you, inside another tool
reaching your data


The API
a program
the same operation, many times




The first three all assume a person is present. The fourth is the one that does not.

title: Sunday, September 27
text:
Why call it directly


Repetition
The same judgment applied to five thousand rows. Nobody is going to paste them one at a time.


Software
The model becomes a component inside something else, with your instructions fixed and the user’s input as the variable.


Control
You pick the model, the temperature, and the system prompt, and they do not change under you.


Cost
You pay per token rather than per seat, which is cheaper for bursts and dearer for constant use.

title: Sunday, September 27
text:
The request
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()          # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY

resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5",
    max_tokens=500,
    system="You classify customer complaints. Answer with one word.",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "The unit arrived cracked."}],
)

print(resp.content[0].text)
Everything in that call is something you chose: the model, the ceiling on output, the instructions, and the input.

title: Sunday, September 27
text:
The key


Create a key in the console. It is shown once.
Put it in an environment variable, not in the code.
Never commit it. A key in a public repository is found in minutes.
Set a spending limit on the key before you use it in a loop.



Step 4 is the one people skip. A loop over a large file with a bug in the exit condition spends real money.

title: Sunday, September 27
text:
What you are charged for

Input tokens and output tokens, priced separately, per million.








Input
everything you send — instructions, tool definitions, the whole conversation so far


Output
only what comes back



A conversation costs more each turn because the entire history is sent again every time. In an agent loop, every tool result joins that history.

title: Sunday, September 27
text:
First calls
Exercise 18 · 30 minutes


Put your key in the environment and make one call that returns a sentence.
Change the system prompt and make the same call. Note what moved.
Run the same request three times at temperature 1, then three times at 0.
Now loop it: classify 200 rows of a CSV, one call per row, and write the results to a new column.
Report what it cost.



Record the cost of step 4 per row. Fifty thousand rows is that number times two hundred and fifty.

title: Sunday, September 27
text: The loop

title: Sunday, September 27
text:
What an agent is, exactly


A model
Which one, and at what temperature.


A system prompt
What it is for, and what it refuses.


A tool list
Everything it can do. Nothing else is possible.


A permission mode
Which actions stop for approval.


A place to run
A machine, a directory, a network.


A loop
Call, execute, feed the result back, repeat.


There is no seventh ingredient.

title: Sunday, September 27
text:
Three kinds of tools




Where the code is
Example




Built in
in the harness
read a file, run a command, fetch a page


Yours
a function you wrote
look up a customer in your system


Someone else’s
an MCP server
the Northwind database, EIA, FRED



All three arrive at the model the same way: a name, a description, and a parameter schema.

title: Sunday, September 27
text:
A tool you write
@tool("order_total",
      "Total revenue for one order. Takes an order id.",
      {"order_id": int})
async def order_total(args):
    df = pd.read_excel("northwind_orderdetails.xlsx")
    rows = df[df.OrderID == args["order_id"]]
    total = (rows.UnitPrice * rows.Quantity).sum()
    return {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": f"${total:,.2f}"}]}
The description is the interface. The model never sees the code.

title: Sunday, September 27
text:
Build one
Exercise 19 · 75 minutes · three stages


A chatbot with no tools at all. Ask it how many files are in the directory it is running in. Read the answer carefully.
Give it one built-in tool — reading files — and ask again.
Write a tool of your own over data you brought or the order spreadsheets. Give it a system prompt that says what it is for.



In stage 1 the model has no way to see the directory. Keep its answer — you compare it against stage 2.

title: Sunday, September 27
text:
What stage 1 shows

Asked a question about a filesystem it cannot reach, a model with no tools still answers.


It produces a plausible number
It produces plausible filenames
Nothing in the output is marked as unavailable

The same model with a file-reading tool answers correctly. What changed is not the model. It is that something connected the question to the directory.

title: Sunday, September 27
text: Choosing what it can do

title: Sunday, September 27
text:
Narrow beats capable

What you leave out of the tool list is not a limitation. It is the security model.





A general agent
A narrow agent




Tool list
everything
three tools


Runs as
you
a service account


Reaches
your whole machine
one dataset


Right for
your own work
anything you hand to someone else




Buy for yourself; build for other people.

title: Sunday, September 27
section: An agent whose tool is an agent
text:
An agent whose tool is an agent


An orchestrator receives the question and holds no data of its own.
It calls a research agent that can read the public web and nothing private.
It calls a data agent that can read your database and cannot reach the internet.
It assembles the answer from what both returned.


The two workers never share a context. Neither one holds private data and an outbound channel at the same time — which is the point of the arrangement, and the subject of the rest of this morning.

title: Sunday, September 27
section: Talk it out of its job
text:
Talk it out of its job
Exercise 20 · 25 minutes


Take the narrow agent you just built.
Ask it something outside its purpose. See whether the system prompt holds.
Now ask persuasively — a plausible reason, an appeal to an exception, an instruction that claims to come from you.
Note which refusals came from the prompt and which came from a tool that does not exist.



Keep what you found. Some of it is the first item after the break.

title: Sunday, September 27
text:
Screen shares

What your agent is for, in one sentence
Its tool list, read out loud
The one thing you could talk it into # 13 · Managing security risks

Believing it, sending it out, and letting it act.

title: Sunday, September 27
text:
Three risks


Believing it
A wrong number, delivered fluently. Friday morning was this one.


Sending data out
Your material reaching a third party. A contract problem.


Letting it act
An agent doing something on your behalf that you did not ask for. An engineering problem.


Most corporate AI policy addresses the second one only.

title: Sunday, September 27
text: Sending data out

title: Sunday, September 27
text:
What a contract gives you









What it adds
Enough for




Opt out of training
a setting, revocable, data still retained briefly
personal, non-sensitive work


A signed DPA
liability, breach notice, audit rights, a subprocessor list
client data, regulated data


A DPA plus a BAA
the same, covering protected health information
anything under HIPAA


An enterprise agreement
SLAs, support, SSO, capacity
scale and operations




The last row buys operations. The privacy terms are the same as the row above it.

title: Sunday, September 27
text:
What the regulation actually requires


HIPAA
Satisfactory assurances “must be documented through a written contract” meeting §164.504(e).
A BAA is required, not advisable. 45 CFR 164.502(e).

SEC Reg S-P
Written policies “reasonably designed to require oversight, including through due diligence and monitoring, of service providers.”
17 CFR 248.30.

title: Sunday, September 27
section: Run it where the data already is
text:
Run it where the data already is




AWS
Google Cloud
Azure




Claude
Bedrock
Vertex AI
Foundry


GPT
Bedrock

Azure AI Foundry


Gemini

native




If the data already sits in one of those, the model can run inside the same perimeter. No new vendor, no new trust boundary, and the DPA you already signed still applies.

title: Sunday, September 27
section: When the contract is not enough
text:
When the contract is not enough


Send less — a schema and a few synthetic rows rather than the table.
Anonymize — strip the names, the account numbers, the identifiers.
Run a smaller model on your own hardware, so nothing leaves at all.



A DPA is a promise backed by liability. These three are physical facts about where the data went.

title: Sunday, September 27
text: Letting it act

title: Sunday, September 27
text:
Prompt injection

The model cannot tell an instruction from a piece of content. Both arrive as text in the same conversation.

Text placed where the agent will read it — an email, a document, a web page, a spreadsheet cell — is read in the same way as text you typed. An attacker needs no credentials, only a way to get words in front of the model.

OWASP has ranked this first among risks to LLM applications since 2025.

title: Sunday, September 27
text:
EchoLeak
CVE-2025-32711 · Microsoft 365 Copilot · June 2025


An attacker mails the victim a message containing instructions invisible to a human reader.
The victim asks Copilot to summarize their email. Copilot reads the hidden instructions.
Following them, Copilot places confidential data inside a URL in its response.
The victim’s browser fetches that URL automatically.
The attacker reads the data out of their own server log.


Zero clicks by the victim beyond the summary request.

title: Sunday, September 27
text:
Three legs


Private data
Something worth taking: client records, financials, an inbox.


Untrusted content
Text an outsider can control: a web page, an email, an uploaded file.


An outbound channel
Any way for text to leave: fetching a URL, sending mail, writing somewhere shared.


All three in one agent is the condition. Remove any one and the attack has nowhere to go.

title: Sunday, September 27
section: The question to ask about any deployment
text:
The question to ask about any deployment


The check

Does this agent hold private data, read content an outsider can influence, and have a way to send text out — at the same time?

It is answerable from an architecture diagram, without knowing anything about how the model works.

title: Sunday, September 27
text:
Red-team a classmate’s agent
Exercise 21 · 45 minutes


Swap agents with someone. You get their code and their tool list.
Diagram it: what private data can it reach, what untrusted text does it read, how could text leave.
Plant an injection in something it will read — a file, a row, a page it fetches.
Try to make it act on the injection. Record what worked and what it refused.
Give the author two changes: one to the prompt, one to the tool list. Say which one you would actually rely on.



Use synthetic data. Nothing in this exercise touches anything real.

title: Sunday, September 27
section: Making it impossible rather than unlikely
text: Making it impossible rather than unlikely

title: Sunday, September 27
section: Two ways to stop the same thing
text:
Two ways to stop the same thing


Governance
Every call is inspected as it is made and allowed or refused.
Works on the calls you anticipated. Judgment happens at run time, every time.

Isolation
The route does not exist.
Works on calls nobody anticipated. Nothing is judged, because nothing is possible.


Real systems use both. The order matters: isolate first, then govern what remains.

title: Sunday, September 27
text:
The split


The agent that reads untrusted content gets no private data and no credentials.
The agent that holds private data has no route to the internet.
An orchestrator calls both as tools and never exposes one to the other’s context.


Neither worker ever holds all three legs. That property is a fact about the network and the tool lists, not a rule either agent has been asked to follow.

title: Sunday, September 27
text:
Your container, as an example



Filesystem
its own — no other student’s files exist inside it


Processes
its own — you cannot see anyone else’s


Network
its own namespace, and it cannot reach a peer container


The gate
your terminal sits behind your own login



You spent four days inside a working example of the pattern.

title: Sunday, September 27
text: Monday

title: Sunday, September 27
text:
Write the plan
Exercise 22 · 40 minutes
One page, covering:


The workflow. Who does it now, how often, and how long it takes.
What you would build — a skill, an app, or an agent — and who uses it.
The data it touches, and where that data lives today.
The tool list, written out. What it can do and what it deliberately cannot.
The three-leg check, answered.
What it costs to run, and what has to be true for it to be worth that.

title: Sunday, September 27
text:
Pitches
35 minutes
Three minutes each. The room responds as the people who would have to approve it, fund it, or use it.
For each plan, someone in the room names:

The step that will not survive contact with the real workflow
The one item on the tool list they would remove

title: Sunday, September 27
text:
What you have


A habit
Describe the data, require the code, check the counts, reconcile a second way.


A file
A skill, published, that a colleague can install in two commands.


A question
Private data, untrusted content, an outbound channel — asked of anything before it is switched on.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Morning
text:
This morning

Yesterday ended with a number you could defend. This morning it becomes something somebody else can open.



Creating docs
Excel, Word and PowerPoint out of the machine — including into the template your firm already uses.


Creating apps
How software actually works, then build one, then put it on the internet.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Morning
text:
Office files are archives

A .docx, .xlsx or .pptx is a ZIP file containing XML.

Unzip one and the document’s structure, styles and data are readable as text. That is why an agent can edit an existing file in place — keeping its template, its headers and its formatting — instead of rebuilding it.

So “edit the deck the firm already uses” opens the existing file, while “build me a deck like ours” starts from nothing.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Morning
section: Excel that is a model, not a table
text:
Excel that is a model, not a table


A table
Values pasted into cells. Change an assumption and the analysis is rerun somewhere else, by you.

A model
Inputs in labelled cells, formulas referencing them, a chart bound to the range. Change an assumption in the sheet and everything moves.

Ask for formulas rather than values, and name the input cells.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Morning
text:
What the recipient opens








Recipient
Format
What it has to carry




An analyst who will extend it
.xlsx with formulas
inputs, formulas, the definition


A manager approving something
.pptx or one page
the number, the chart, the caveat


A job that runs every week
.csv plus a script
reproducibility, not formatting


The record
.docx or PDF
the method, in sentences

title: Saturday, September 26 · Morning
section: The deck already has a house style
text:
The deck already has a house style

Asking for “a deck in our style” produces something that looks approximately right and is wrong in every detail a partner will notice.

A .pptx template is not a picture of a design. It is a file holding named slide layouts, a theme with the firm’s exact colours and fonts, and placeholder positions measured to the point.

Open one with unzip -l. The layouts are in ppt/slideLayouts/, the palette and typefaces in ppt/theme/theme1.xml.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Morning
section: Fill the template, do not imitate it
text:
Fill the template, do not imitate it


Generating a deck
The model invents a layout. Colours are close. The logo is missing, the footer is wrong, and the title sits four points off.

Filling a template
The file is opened, a named layout is chosen, and text goes into the placeholders that layout defines. Everything else is inherited.

Same request, two implementations. The second is the one you can send to a client.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Morning
section: A skill that knows your template
text:
A skill that knows your template


Put the .pptx in the skill’s folder. The template is an asset, not a description.
List the layouts by name, and say in prose what each one is for.
Say which placeholder takes what — title, body, source line, page number.
State the rules a human would know: how many bullets before a slide splits, where the source line goes, what never gets edited.




Prompt

Read template.pptx. List every slide layout by name and index, and for each one the placeholders it defines with their type and position. Write that into SKILL.md as a table, then write the instructions for filling it.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Morning
section: Turn your own template into a skill
text:
Turn your own template into a skill
Exercise 10 · 40 minutes


Upload a deck your firm actually uses. Any recent one will do.
Have the layouts and placeholders enumerated, and check the list against what you see in PowerPoint.
Write the skill, with the file in its folder.
Build a three-slide deck from yesterday’s country analysis using it.
Open the result next to a real deck and find what is off.



Step 5 finds the thing the template cannot carry — usually a rule that lives in somebody’s head rather than in the file.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Morning
text:
Build the deliverable
Exercise 11 · 30 minutes


Take your corrected country analysis.
Produce it in the format the person who would receive it actually opens.
Put the revenue definition and the row counts on the face of it.
Open the file in the file browser and look at it the way they would.



If you built a workbook, change one input cell and check that the chart moves.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Morning
section: When a skill is not enough
text:
When a skill is not enough


A skill
For someone who has the agent, the files, and a reason to be at a command line.

An app
For someone with a browser and a question. No install, no terminal, no account.

Same job, different audience. Which one you build follows from who is going to run it.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Morning
text:
Frontend and backend


Frontend
The browser. HTML, CSS and JavaScript — it draws the page and collects the clicks.

Backend
A program on a server that listens continuously for requests. Yours will be Python.


You open a URL. The browser sends a GET request. The server sends back HTML, CSS and JavaScript. The browser interprets that and shows you a page.


Right-click any web page and choose View Page Source. That is the frontend code, exactly as the backend handed it over.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Morning
text:
Then you click something

A POST request carries data the other way — a form, a country you typed. The server does what it was written to do and replies.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Morning
text:
Running locally


localhost
127.0.0.1 is the loopback address. The browser asks the machine it is already running on, and the request never reaches a network.


Ports
One machine runs many programs listening at once. The port number tells the operating system which of them gets the request.


You write the app as a .py file. FastAPI writes one; uvicorn runs it and starts it listening on a port.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Morning
text:
Three shapes


One page, no server
Everything runs in the browser. A single HTML file you can mail to someone.


A small server
Python behind the page. Needed when there is a database, a key, or a file to write.


A server that calls a model
The page collects a question; the server sends it to the model with your key, not the user’s.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Morning
text:
One page, no server
Exercise 12 · 25 minutes


Build a single HTML file that does one useful calculation from your own work.
Open it in the browser from the file browser. No server involved.
Mail it to yourself and open it on your phone.



This is the shape most business tools should be and almost never are. Nothing to deploy, nothing to break, nothing to pay for.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Morning
section: A page with Python behind it
text:
A page with Python behind it
Exercise 13 · 40 minutes


Take the country analysis. Put a dropdown of countries on a page.
Have the server read the spreadsheets, compute the answer for the country chosen, and return it.
Serve it on port 8000 and open it at your own address on the lab server.
Watch the terminal while you click. Every request appears there.



Step 4 is where GET and POST stop being abstract.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Morning
text:
Hand it to your neighbour
Exercise 14 · 25 minutes


Give your address to the person next to you and say nothing else.
Watch them use it. Write down every place they hesitate.
Fix the one that cost them the most time.
Swap back and check the fix on their machine, not yours.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Morning
text: Deploying an app

title: Saturday, September 26 · Morning
text:
Platform as a service

You hand a host your repository. It builds the app, runs it, and puts it behind a public URL. There is no server for you to administer.

Railway, Render, Koyeb and Heroku all do this. We use Koyeb, which has a free tier.


Create a free account at koyeb.com.
In the control panel, create an API access token. Koyeb shows it once, so copy it then.
Add it to your .env file in the container.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Morning
text:
What has to travel


Prompt

My goal is to push this app to GitHub as a new public repo and then create a Koyeb service connected to it. Walk me through it one step at a time.


The host builds only what is in the repository. Data files you told git to ignore never arrive, and the app fails on a machine you cannot see. Nothing from .env belongs in a public repo — secrets go in Koyeb’s environment settings instead.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Morning
text:
Put it on the internet
Exercise 15 · 45 minutes


Push the app from Exercise 13 to a public GitHub repository.
Create the Koyeb service and watch the build log.
When it fails, read the log before asking. It is almost always a missing file or a missing key.
Open the public URL on your phone, off the lab wifi.
Send the URL to two people in the room.



A custom domain is optional and takes ten minutes: buy one, create an API token at the registrar, and have the DNS record written for you.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Morning
section: What you just learned about deployment
text:
What you just learned about deployment

What runs on your machine does not run anywhere else until you make it
The repository is the unit of deployment, and it is not the same as your folder
Secrets live in the host’s settings, never in the code
The build log says what went wrong, in order, every time

title: Saturday, September 26 · Morning
text:
This afternoon
The app you just deployed answers from what you wrote into it. This afternoon it answers from your own documents instead.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
This afternoon


Persistent instructions
Standing rules the agent reads every turn, and tasks written down once.


Connectors and plugins
Tools on somebody else’s server, and folders of skills other people published.


Agent harnesses
Claude Code is one program around the model. What the others decided differently.


Four hands-on blocks. By six you will have written a skill, connected to data you do not hold, and installed plugins other people wrote.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
The repeated instruction

This morning you typed the same four things into every prompt: describe the data first, show the code, report row counts, reconcile a second way.

Each of those is a standing instruction about how you want work done. Typing them into each prompt makes them optional, and one of them gets left out at four in the afternoon.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
section: Everything arrives as one block of text
text:
Everything arrives as one block of text
Each turn, the harness assembles the request from parts you can control:



Part
Set by
When it is sent




System prompt
the tool
every turn


Tool definitions
the tool and your config
every turn


CLAUDE.md
you
every turn


Skill descriptions
you
every turn, one line each


A skill’s body
you
only when that skill is used


The conversation
you and the tools
growing, every turn

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
The cost of always

A file read on every turn is paid for on every turn — in money, in latency, and in the model’s attention.



CLAUDE.md
Short and always present. Standing rules that apply to everything you do in that folder.


A skill
One line always present — its description. The body arrives only when the description matches what you asked for.


A CLAUDE.md that runs to three thousand words is paid for on every turn, including the turns none of it applies to.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
What belongs in each


Standing rules

How you want numbers handled
What the folders hold
Conventions everything here follows
Anything you have corrected twice



Not standing rules

Steps for one particular task
Anything longer than a page
Background that can be looked up
A tool you use once a month

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
Write your standing rules
Exercise 5 · 30 minutes


Create ~/CLAUDE.md in your container.
Write the four rules from this morning in your own words, and two more of your own.
Start a new conversation and give it a task that would break one of the rules.
Change a rule and watch the behavior change.



Ask it to name the rules it is following. If it cannot, the file is not being read.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text: Skills

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
A skill is a folder
country-report/
  SKILL.md          the instructions
  references/       longer material, read only when needed
  scripts/          code the skill runs rather than regenerates
SKILL.md opens with two lines of metadata and then plain prose:
---
name: country-report
description: Build the monthly revenue-by-country report from the
  order spreadsheets. Use when asked for the country report, the
  monthly revenue rollup, or revenue by market.
---

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
The description is the trigger


Does not fire
“Helps with reporting.”

Fires
“Build the monthly revenue-by-country report from the order spreadsheets. Use when asked for the country report, the monthly revenue rollup, or revenue by market.”

The description is the only part of a skill always in front of the model, and it decides whether the rest is ever read. Write the words the person asking would use.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
What goes in the body


What the task produces, stated first.
Where the inputs are, by path.
The steps in order, including the checks.
What to do when something is missing.
What the output looks like when it is right.



Prose, not pseudocode. The reader is a model that already knows Python and does not know your files.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
Scripts beat instructions


Instructions
The code is written fresh each time. Same intent, a different implementation, different bugs.

A script
The code is written once and tested. The skill says when to run it and what the arguments mean.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
Three ways to invoke









How
When




Slash command
/country-report
you know exactly what you want


By name
“use the country report skill”
you are half sure


Automatically
“build me the March rollup”
the description matched



The third only happens if the description was written for it.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
Already in your container



Skill
What it does




xlsx
builds and edits Excel workbooks, with formulas and charts


docx
the same for Word, including templates


pptx
the same for PowerPoint, including an existing deck


finance-data
pulls prices, fundamentals and macro series


web-app
scaffolds an app you can serve on port 8000


skill-creator
writes and tests a new skill



Open one. It is the same kind of file you are about to write.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
Write a skill
Exercise 6 · 50 minutes


Pick something you do at work more than once a month, with inputs and a shape.
Run /skill-creator and work through it, answering in your own vocabulary.
Put a real input file in the container and run the skill on it.
In a fresh conversation, ask for the task in the words a colleague would use.
Fix the description until it fires.



Step 4 is the test. A skill that fires only when you name it has not been described yet.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
The problem a standard solves

Every tool wants to reach every data source. Without a standard, that is one integration per pair.



N × M integrations without a protocol


N + M with one


A server written for nothing in particular is reachable from every client that speaks the protocol.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
What a connector actually sends


The client connects to the server and asks what it offers.
The server returns a list of tools: each with a name, a description in English, and the parameters it takes.
That list goes into the model’s context alongside its built-in tools.
The model asks for one by name. The client calls the server and puts the result back in the conversation.



The model does not know a connector from a built-in tool. Both are entries in the same list.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
section: Where the call is made from
text:
Where the call is made from

In Claude Cowork, and in most setups a firm will hand you, the machine the agent’s shell runs on has no route to the internet. The connector works anyway.



At the shell
curl https://api.stlouisfed.org/...
Refused. Everything leaving that machine passes a proxy that allows a short list of addresses, and that is not one of them.

Through the connector
fred_get_observations("UNRATE")
Rows come back. Same machine, same second, same model.


Because your machine never places the call. The client end sits outside it, calls FRED itself, and hands the rows back into the conversation. Your key goes with it and is never on the machine to steal.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
section: A narrower door, not a hole
text:
A narrower door, not a hole


Open the network instead
Allow the machine to reach stlouisfed.org and it can send anything to any address there, in any form it likes.

Leave it shut, add a connector
It can call run_sql with a SELECT. That is the entire new capability.

The connector is the smaller of the two. That is why the network stays off and the connector goes on, and not the other way around.

It costs something. The connector reaches out from outside the sandbox holding your credentials, so a sentence in a file it reads can ask for that call. Cutting the machine off from the network did not cut off the connector. Sunday morning.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
Servers you can connect today



Server
Address
Sign-in




Northwind orders
northwind-mcp.rice-business.org/mcp
none


Energy data (EIA)
eia.rice-business.org/mcp
none

Same three servers, reachable from Claude Code in your container and from Claude Desktop on your laptop. Neither was written for either one.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
Connect one
Exercise 7 · 40 minutes


Connect the Northwind server, and then one of the two data services.
Ask what tools each one offers, and read the descriptions.
Ask the Northwind server which countries generated the most revenue, and have it show the SQL.
Ask something that needs the connector and a file in your container at the same time.
Try to make the database server do something other than read.



Keep that number. Tomorrow you compute it yourself from spreadsheets and reconcile the two.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text: Where the limit lives

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
Read-only, enforced four ways



Where
What refuses




The database
a role without write permission


The application
a whitelist of allowed operations


The connector
run_sql rejecting anything that is not a SELECT


The tool list
no write tool exists to call



The model is not consulted at any of them. That is the property that makes them worth having.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
Instructions are not a limit


A rule in a prompt
“Never modify the database.”
Text in a conversation, competing with other text in the same conversation.

A tool that does not exist
There is nothing to call.
No wording reaches it, because nothing is being persuaded.


Everything you can talk it out of was a request, not a constraint.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
Mail and calendar

The same shape applied to an inbox: an agent that reads everything and sends nothing.



It reads
Threads, calendar entries, attachments. Enough to tell you what is waiting and what it is about.


It drafts
Replies, parked where you can read them.


It does not send
No send tool, no delete tool. Sending stays a thing you do.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
section: Why that split is the whole design
text:
Why that split is the whole design
An agent reading your mail is holding two things at once: your private correspondence, and text written by people outside your organization.
Give it an outbound channel and those two facts combine into a third. We come back to this on Sunday, in detail.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text: Installing plugins

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
What you install

A plugin is a folder somebody else published. Installing it adds their work to your Claude in one step.



What it can carry
Skills, slash commands, subagents, hooks, and MCP servers.


What you get
Every file and script in it, without being told which ones to copy where.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
Two commands
/plugin marketplace add kerryback/skills
/plugin install finance-data@kerryback
The first points Claude at a public repository holding an index of plugins. The second installs one of them. /plugin on its own lists what you have.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
section: A marketplace you can use today
text:
A marketplace you can use today
kerryback/skills holds fifteen. Seven worth your time:







finance-data
prices, fundamentals, SEC filings and macro series, as CSV


elegant-pdf
branded flyers, programs and reports as print-quality PDF


critique
parallel reviewers on work Claude produced, and what to do


human-write
prose that does not read as machine-generated


shoji2
Quarto slide decks in the theme these slides use


voiceover
a narrated MP4 and transcript from a deck


smithers
a read-only desk over your mail and calendar

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
Read it before you install

An installed plugin runs with your permissions, on your machine, against your files.



Open the repository and read the SKILL.md of anything you are about to install.
Check what it runs: a script, a command, an MCP server reaching outside.
Install into a container first when you are not sure.



Same question as Sunday morning’s, asked earlier: what can it reach, and what can leave.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
Install and try
Exercise 8 · 40 minutes


Add the kerryback/skills marketplace and list what is in it.
Install two plugins that look useful for your own work.
Run one of them on your own data or your own document.
Open its SKILL.md and read how it does what it does.
Say what you would change, and what you would have written differently.



You wrote one of these earlier. Step 4 is reading somebody else’s.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
Four rungs




Where it lives
Who has it




A prompt
in your head
you, when you remember


CLAUDE.md
one folder
anyone working in that folder


A skill
a file
you, everywhere, when it matches


A plugin
a repository someone published
anyone who installs it



The same instruction each time, moved somewhere that outlasts the conversation.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
Same model, different program
The model is a string in a config file. Everything you experience as “the tool” is the program wrapped around it: what it sends each turn, which tools it offers, how it asks permission, and where it runs.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
section: The harness is the other five
text:
The harness is the other five

You pick the model. Everything else on that list is supplied by the program around it.

Buying a harness — Claude Code, or one of the open ones — is buying somebody’s answers to those five questions. The answers are not the same, and this year they stopped being the same in ways that show up in the output.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
What actually differs








The question it answers




Model coupling
one vendor’s models, or any provider you can point it at


Context
what gets sent each turn, and what happens when the window fills


Tool surface
four tools, or forty


Permissions
how it stops — approval rules, an OS sandbox, or a container


Extension
plugins, MCP servers, skills, instruction files


Where it lives
a terminal, an editor, a web page, or a library you import




Every one of these is a design choice somebody made and wrote down. None of them is the model.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
The open field








Claude Code
Anthropic models only
the reference implementation


Codex
OpenAI models only
Rust; OS-level sandbox by default


OpenCode
75+ providers
the mature open alternative; per-agent permissions


DeepSeek Harness
any provider
everything is a plugin, including the loop


Pi
any provider
four tools and a very short prompt


Goose · OpenHands
any provider
neutral governance; container-first


Gemini CLI · Qwen Code
their own models
vendor CLIs on the same pattern



Everything but Claude Code is open source, MIT or Apache — you can read the loop. Two of those still only talk to their maker’s models.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
Thick or thin


Claude Code
Forty-plus tools. A layered system prompt with a cached boundary. Four fallback strategies when the context fills. Subagents that fork and run in the background.
The harness does a great deal on your behalf, and you did not write any of it.

Pi
Four tools — read, write, edit, run a command. A system prompt under a thousand tokens. No subagents, no plan mode, no MCP.
Anything else, the agent writes for itself as an extension while you watch.


Databricks benchmarked both and found the thin one matched or beat the thick one at a fraction of the cost, because it sent roughly three times less context per turn.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
The permission model



Harness
How it stops you




Claude Code
rules you configure, checked before each call


Codex
the operating system — Seatbelt on macOS, Landlock on Linux


OpenHands
a Docker container the agent cannot leave


Cline
a human clicking approve, every time


OpenCode
per-agent tool permissions, granted once and remembered




The distinction from this morning, in a different form: a mode that asks you, versus a boundary that makes the call impossible. Two of these five are the second kind.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
section: Why any of this is on the slide
text:
Why any of this is on the slide

A benchmark number is a model and a harness together. Change the harness and the number moves.



The same model scores differently under two harnesses on the same benchmark.
Papers report the model and omit the harness.
Removing most of an agent’s tools has been shown to raise its score, not lower it.
So a leaderboard tells you less than it appears to.


When somebody tells you a model can or cannot do something, the useful question is what it was wearing at the time.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Afternoon
text:
Tomorrow
Everything today has been about setting the agent up. Tomorrow you point it at data and find out whether you can trust what comes back.

Course Description
Generative AI moved into ordinary business work faster than any recent technology. McKinsey’s global survey found the share of organizations regularly using generative AI in at least one business function rose from roughly a third in 2023 to about two-thirds a year later, and higher still since. The Census Bureau’s Business Trends and Outlook Survey, which asks the narrower question of whether a firm used AI to produce a good or service in the past two weeks, shows the rate roughly doubling over the same period, with adoption concentrated in information and professional services. The gap between those two numbers is itself informative: many people are using these tools, and far fewer organizations have built anything durable around them.
Business uses fall into a few broad categories. There is individual productivity — the drafting, summarizing, analysis, and coding that one person does faster with a model beside them. There is internal deployment — putting a model to work on the firm’s own documents and systems, in workflows that several people depend on. There are customer-facing applications, where the model talks to people outside the firm. And there is the reshaping of the product itself, where AI is what is being sold rather than what makes it. The categories differ less in the technology than in what goes wrong: a bad answer you catch yourself is a nuisance, a bad answer inside a workflow is a process failure, and a bad answer in front of a customer is a liability.
This course covers the first two. We start with individual productivity, because the judgment you need there — knowing what the model is doing, what it is good at, how it fails, and how to check it — is the same judgment every larger deployment rests on. We then move to work that outlives the session you did it in: writing a repeated task down so others can run it, connecting a model to data it was never trained on, generating the document or application someone else opens, and assembling an agent with a deliberately chosen list of things it can do. The course closes on the questions a firm has to answer before switching any of this on — where the data goes, what an outside document can talk the system into doing, and what it costs to run.
The course is hands-on throughout. You work in your own container on the course lab server, and you show what you built to the room.


Learning Objectives
By the end of the course, you should be able to:

Work fluently with generative AI in your own tasks — choosing the right tool for the job, directing it well, and verifying what it gives back, with a working understanding of how these models produce their answers and where that mechanism fails.
Turn ad hoc use into something durable — a documented procedure, a connection to your own data, a deliverable someone else opens, or an agent with a defined job — that a colleague can run without you.
Evaluate a proposed deployment on the terms a firm actually decides on: which model and where it runs, what data it touches, what it is permitted to do, and what it costs relative to what it saves.
Recognize and contain the risks that come with letting a model act — confidentiality, prompt injection, and the exfiltration of data through the system’s own channels — and say what would have to be true for a deployment to be safe rather than merely lucky.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
text:
This morning


How the model works
Tokens, vectors, one prediction at a time, and what training added on top.


Chat, CLI, and sandbox
The same model reached from a chat window, a command line, and a machine you were given.


Prompting tips
Planning, requiring code for numbers, and checking what comes back.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
text:
Tokenization
Text is cut into pieces from a fixed vocabulary before the model sees any of it.
"The cat sat on the mat"  ->  ["The", " cat", " sat", " on", " the", " mat"]

"Unbelievable"            ->  ["Un", "believ", "able"]
Common words stay whole; rare and long words break into pieces. A typical vocabulary runs to about 100,000 tokens.

Numbers break on the same rules, which have nothing to do with arithmetic. 13,963,378.65 reaches the model as a handful of unrelated pieces.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
text:
The whole task

Given the tokens so far, predict the token that comes next. That is the entire operation.

Everything a model appears to do — answering, summarizing, writing code, refusing — is that one prediction, repeated.

The input can currently run to about a million tokens, roughly two-thirds of the Harry Potter saga. That context window has grown a thousandfold since GPT-3 in 2020.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
text:
Vectors
The model does not work with tokens. It works with numbers.


Each token is a list
“king” becomes 4,096 numbers. “queen” becomes 4,096 numbers that are close to them.
Tokens used in similar contexts end up near each other.


The space is mostly empty
There are far more possible vectors than there are tokens, so most points in the space name nothing.
The prediction can land between tokens.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
section: A neural network is a function
text:
A neural network is a function


The idea
\(y = 4x\) is a function. The 4 is a parameter.
Change it to 3 and you have the same structure with different behavior.

The scale
Same idea with hundreds of billions of parameters, arranged as a transformer — the architecture published by Google researchers in 2017.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
text:
Training


What is learned
The vector for every token, and every parameter in the network.
Both are adjusted together to reduce prediction error on the training text.


What it takes
Trillions of words. Thousands of GPUs for weeks or months. Tens to hundreds of millions of dollars for one run.



Nothing is looked up or stored as fact. The arrangement captures how words are used, which is why it recalls common things reliably and rare things unreliably.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
text:
The pipeline


Tokenize the input.
Look up the vector for each token.
Feed the vectors into the network.
The network produces one output vector.
Find which token vectors are closest to it.
Emit a token, append it to the input, and start again at step 1.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
text:
Temperature
The network does not output one token. It outputs a probability for every token in the vocabulary. Temperature controls how that distribution is sampled.



Setting
Behavior




Near 0
The highest-probability token every time. Repeatable.


Near 1
Sampled from the distribution. Different each run.


Higher
Low-probability tokens get picked. Text degrades.




In a chatbot, including Claude Desktop, temperature is fixed near 1 and you cannot change it. Through the API you can.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
text:
From prediction to conversation
A model trained only to predict the next token continues your text. It does not answer a question.


Role tokens. The text is wrapped in markers: <|user|> your question <|assistant|>.
Instruction tuning. The model is further trained on examples where what follows <|assistant|> is a useful reply.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback. Raters score replies, and the model is trained toward what raters preferred.


The mechanism did not change. What changed is which continuation is the likely one.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
text:
Reasoning models
The same trick applied again: train the model to write out its working before it answers.


How it was trained
Reinforcement learning on problems whose answers can be checked — mathematics, code, puzzles — rewarding the chains of tokens that arrived at a correct answer.


Why it helps
The model holds no state between tokens. The intermediate tokens are the only place a partial result can live, so writing them out is the computation.



The thinking you see may be a summary of a much longer chain, and you are charged for the whole chain as output tokens.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
text:
What thinking longer buys


Moves
Problems that decompose: multi-step arithmetic, code that has to satisfy several constraints, planning a sequence of actions.

Does not move
Recall of a fact it never learned, questions of taste, and anything where the first token was already right.

More tokens at answer time, rather than a larger model, is the dial. You pay for it in latency and in output tokens.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
text:
What that explains


Fluent and wrong
Plausible text is exactly what the objective rewards. Correct text is a side effect of plausible text usually being correct.


Confident either way
Nothing in the mechanism distinguishes a recalled fact from a well-formed guess.


Arithmetic
Predicting the digits of a sum is a different operation from adding. Code does the second.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
section: Ask the same thing three ways
text:
Ask the same thing three ways

“Here are four spreadsheets of orders. Which countries generated the most revenue?”








Door
What happens




Chat in a browser
You upload the files. It answers in the window.


Claude Code on your laptop
It opens the files where they sit, writes code, saves a chart next to them.


Claude Code in a container
The same, on a machine that is not yours, holding nothing but what you put there.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
text:
Same model, different harness


The model
Identical in all three. Same weights, same training, same tendencies.
It has no memory of you, no filesystem, and no way to run anything.

The harness
The program around the model: what tools it offers, what it puts in front of the model each turn, and what it does with the answer.
Everything that differs between the three doors is here.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
text:
Sign in
Exercise 1 · 20 minutes


Go to lab803.kerryback.com and sign in with the username and password you were mailed.
Open the tab labelled Claude. You are at a command line inside a container that belongs only to you.
Type ls and then pwd. Note where you are.
Ask it, in English: what files are in this folder, and what can you reach on this machine?
Read the answer against what you saw in step 3.



Three tabs: a Claude terminal, a plain terminal, and a file browser. Port 8000 is yours for anything you serve.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
text:
Which tools each door offers









Chat in a browser
Claude Code




Write and run code
yes, in a sandbox
yes, on the machine


Read your files
what you upload
anything it has permission to open


Search and fetch the web
yes
yes


Run shell commands
no
yes


Install software
no
yes


Use your credentials
no
whatever is on that machine

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
text:
Permissions


Ask
Every action that changes something stops for approval. The default.


Accept edits
File edits go through; commands still stop.


Bypass
Nothing stops. Reasonable in a container that holds nothing you would miss.


The permission mode and the tool list are two different limits. One asks you each time; the other decides what is possible at all.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
text:
What this door reaches
Exercise 2 · 25 minutes


Ask it to count how many files are in the container and how large they are altogether.
Ask it to install a Python package it does not have, then use it.
Ask a question it can only answer by running something — the size of the largest file, the number of lines in the longest one.


Watch what appears between your question and the answer: the command it chose, the output it got back, and what it did with output it did not expect.

Write down the first command that failed and what it did next.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
section: Why a machine of its own
text: Why a machine of its own

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
text:
It runs as you

An agent on your laptop has your filesystem, your network, your VPN, your saved logins, and your keys.

That is what makes it useful for your own work, and it is the reason the same setup is hard to hand to anyone else. There is no boundary between the task you asked for and everything else you can reach.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
text:
What a container changes


Your laptop
Everything you have access to.
A mistake reaches the real thing.

Your container
One home directory, the software installed for this course, and outbound internet.
A mistake reaches what you copied in.


Same agent, same model, same permission modes. The difference is the size of what it can touch.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
text:
Your container







Isolation
Its own filesystem, processes, users, and network namespace


Between students
Your container cannot reach any other student’s


Sign-in
Your terminal and files sit behind your own login


Installed
Python, git, Node, and a set of skills we will use later in the week


Yours
~/ and port 8000

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
text:
First data question
Exercise 3 · 30 minutes


In ~/data you have several spreadsheets of orders, customers, and products.
Ask for the schema first: what tables, what columns, how many rows, what date range.
Then ask one question that needs more than one file to answer.
Have it save a chart as a PNG and open it in the file browser.



Four or five of you will show what you got at the end of the block. Have the chart open and be ready to say which files the number came from.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
text:
Plan before executing
Ask for the approach before any work happens, and read it.


Prompt

Before you change anything: tell me how you would do this, what files you would touch, and what could go wrong. Do not start yet.

A plan can be corrected in a sentence. An execution has to be undone in every file it touched.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
text:
Numbers need code

If a number appears in prose and no code produced it, it was predicted.



Prompt

Compute this in Python and show me the code and the output. Do not report a number you did not compute.

The same rule applies to counts, percentages, dates, and anything summed across rows.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
text:
Verify claims


Ask what would falsify it
“What would have to be true for this to be wrong, and how would I check?”


Make it show its source
The file, the row count, the line of code. A citation you can open beats a summary you cannot.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
text:
Generator–critic


Get the first answer.
Start a fresh conversation and give it the answer without the reasoning that produced it.
Ask it to find what is wrong with it.
Take the objections back to the first conversation.


The second conversation has no stake in the first answer, which is the point of separating them.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
text:
What not to do

Accept a number in prose that no code produced
Let it decide the method when you know the method
Ask a question so broad that any answer looks like an answer
Approve a plan you did not read
Assume a second run gives the same result

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
text:
Planning and a critic
Exercise 4 · 30 minutes


Take the question from Exercise 3 and ask for a plan first. Read it before approving.
Run it. Require code for every number.
Open a second terminal, paste the result with none of the working, and ask what is wrong with it.
Bring the objections back and see which survive.



Write down one objection the critic raised that you would not have thought of.

title: Thursday, September 24 · Morning
text:
This afternoon

Everything this morning was you typing into a fresh conversation. This afternoon is how to stop retyping it, and how to give the agent tools that are not on this machine.

title: Friday, September 25
text:
This morning

One question, five spreadsheets, and a morning: which countries generated the most revenue, and how do you know.



Where the data is
What an organization actually holds, which system is the record, and why the copies disagree.


Whether to believe it
The joins, columns and blanks that produce a wrong total with no error message.

title: Friday, September 25
section: “We should point AI at our data”
text:
“We should point AI at our data”


Heard in every company this year

We should point AI at our data.



Which data?


In whose system?


Entered by whom, and when?

title: Friday, September 25
text:
What the surveys say


897 applications in the average enterprise


29% of them connected to anything else


7% of leaders call their data ready for AI



In the same surveys, 19% of data is called siloed or unusable, and 70% of leaders believe their most valuable insights are inside that 19%.

title: Friday, September 25
text:
Where a number actually lives









Holds
Reachable by




The operational system
what is true right now
its own screens


The warehouse
a nightly copy, reshaped for questions
analysts with SQL


A dashboard
four questions somebody chose in 2024
anyone


An extract
one analyst’s copy, as of some Tuesday
whoever they mailed it to


A shared drive
the documents none of the above hold
anyone who can find it

title: Friday, September 25
text:
Four systems, four meanings of “customer”



In this system
A customer is
Identified by




Sales
an organization you might sell to
an account number


Finance
an entity you invoice
a bill-to number


The warehouse
an address you deliver to
a ship-to code


Support
whoever opened the ticket
an email address



Four counts of customers, all correct, none equal.

title: Friday, September 25
section: Why you cannot just query the live system
text:
Why you cannot just query the live system


It is built for writing
Thousands of tiny writes a minute, tuned for that rather than for scanning a year.


Your report competes
A heavy query slows the screen somebody is typing an order into.


It knows one corner
Finance cannot see sales. Neither can see the warehouse.


It holds now
The current address and the current price. Not last year’s.

title: Friday, September 25
section: Three kinds of copy, routinely confused
text:
Three kinds of copy, routinely confused


The warehouse: a governed copy, refreshed on a schedule, with definitions written down.
The extract: a file somebody pulled once, for one question, and never refreshed.
The export: a spreadsheet mailed to someone who now treats it as the source.



Two of the three age silently. The number in the deck was right when it was pulled.

title: Friday, September 25
section: The vocabulary you need for the rest of the day
text:
The vocabulary you need for the rest of the day



System of record
the one place a fact is authoritative


Silo
a store nothing else can reach


Semantics
whether two columns with one name mean one thing


Lineage
where this number came from, through every hop


Quality
blanks, duplicates, and values nobody validates




Every one of these shows up in the next four hours as a reason a total is wrong.

title: Friday, September 25
text:
Five files, one question

Northwind: a supplier of specialty foods to restaurants and delis. 500 orders, 93 customers, 77 products, 8 categories, spanning 2012 to 2023.

Small enough to hold in your head, and shaped like a company a thousand times larger. What you are about to do to it is what an analyst does to the real thing.

title: Friday, September 25
text:
What you are building

Five spreadsheets in ~/data: orders, order details, customers, products, categories. One question — which countries generated the most revenue, and how do you know.


Read all five parts before you start. Part D is the point of the exercise. Get there even if you have to shorten Part C.

title: Friday, September 25
text:
Part A — describe it first
15 minutes
Before any analysis, have it report — with the code shown:


Every file: row count, column names, data types.
The date range of the orders, and whether each date column is a date or a string.
Missing values by column, as counts rather than “a few”.
Which column joins to which, and whether each join is one-to-one or one-to-many.



Write the join map on paper. You will need it in Part D.

title: Friday, September 25
text:
Part B — revenue by country
25 minutes


Compute revenue per order line, then total by the customer’s country.
There are two columns that could be the price. Say in writing which one you used and why.
Report the row count after every merge and compare it to the row count before.
Rank the countries and take the top five.



There is no discount column and no freight column in these files. Whatever you report is price times quantity, and the deliverable has to say so.

title: Friday, September 25
text:
Part C — a deliverable
20 minutes


Option 1
An Excel workbook: the country table on one sheet, a chart, and a cell stating the revenue definition in words.


Option 2
A five-slide deck: the question, the top five, the chart, the definition, and what you checked.


Either one states the revenue definition on its face. A number without its definition cannot be reconciled against anyone else’s.

title: Friday, September 25
text:
Part D — verify it
25 minutes


Recompute the total by a second route — a different tool, a different order of operations, or straight from the raw files with no merges at all.
Reconcile the two to the cent.
If they disagree, find the cause before changing either one.
List three things that could have made your number wrong, and how you ruled each one out.



If the second route reproduces the first to the cent, say so on the deliverable.

title: Friday, September 25
text:
Part E — if you finish
remaining time

Break revenue out by month and by category
Find a month that does not follow the months around it
Say what in the data produces it, and show the rows

title: Friday, September 25
text:
When you are done
Have open and ready to share:

Your number, and the definition behind it
Your chart
Your second route, and what it gave
The three things that could have gone wrong

title: Friday, September 25
text: What went wrong

title: Friday, September 25
section: Four failures that raise no error
text:
Four failures that raise no error


The wrong join
Rows that did not match are dropped. The total is smaller and nothing says so.


The wrong column
Two files use one name for two different things, and the merge keeps both.


The unstated assumption
What counts as revenue, which rows are excluded, which dates are in scope.


Invention
A number in prose that no line of code produced.

title: Friday, September 25
section: What is actually in these files
text:
What is actually in these files



File
Rows





Orders
500
July 2012 to October 2023


Order details
18,976
38 lines per order on average


Customers
93
in 21 countries


Products
77
in 8 categories



Every order line matches a product, an order, and a customer. No merge in this analysis drops a row — which is why you have to check rather than assume.

title: Friday, September 25
text:
Two columns named UnitPrice

Order details carries the price charged. Products carries the list price. Merge them and you get UnitPrice_x and UnitPrice_y.




Priced at
Total revenue




The price charged
$13,963,378.65


The list price
$13,966,340.55



The two answers differ by $2,962 on $14 million. A sanity check on the magnitude passes either way, so nothing about the wrong choice looks wrong.

title: Friday, September 25
text:
The rows with no country


2 customers with a blank country


482 order lines behind them


$373,609 revenue in those lines


Grouping by country drops blank keys by default. The country table still adds up, to a total 2.7% below the real one, and no country is wrong.

title: Friday, September 25
text:
One-to-many

Merge orders into order details and every order appears once per line — on average 38 times.

Sum anything defined per order after that merge and you have counted it 38 times. On these files the multiplier is large enough to notice. On files where the ratio is 1.2, it is not.

The check is one line: row count before the merge, row count after.

title: Friday, September 25
text:
Dates

03/04/2023 is March 4 or April 3 depending on who wrote the file
A date column read as text sorts 10/01 before 2/01
These orders carry a time as well as a date, so a filter on equality matches nothing
A date read out of Excel can arrive as a serial number

Ask which columns are date types and which are strings, before grouping by month.

title: Friday, September 25
text:
Missing values



How it is written
What a naive count does




An empty cell
usually skipped


0
included in the average


NA, N/A, -, unknown
makes the whole column text


A sentinel such as -999
included, silently



A numeric column that is text because of four N/A cells concatenates where you expected a sum.

title: Friday, September 25
text:
Recompute another way


The same question by a different route through the data.
The same question in a different tool — SQL against the same files, or a pivot table.
The same question in a fresh conversation that has not seen the first answer.


Each route drops different rows and rounds at different points. Agreement across them narrows what can still be wrong.

title: Friday, September 25
section: Make it read its own code
text:
Make it read its own code


Prompt

Here is code and the answer it produced. Ignore the answer. Read the code and tell me what it actually computes — including what it drops and what it assumes.

A fresh conversation reading code has nothing invested in the number already on the screen.

title: Friday, September 25
text:
Find the bug
Exercise 9 · 40 minutes


~/data/planted/country_report.py produces a country table. Its total is wrong.
Read it first and predict where the number goes wrong. Do not run it yet.
Now run it, find the actual causes, and say how much each one moves the total.
Fix them and reconcile against your own Part B number.



There is more than one defect, and they move the total in different directions.

title: Friday, September 25
text:
Tomorrow
Today the answer was a number you checked. Tomorrow it becomes a document somebody else opens, and then an application they use without you.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Afternoon
text:
This afternoon


Retrieval augmented generation
Answering from your own documents, with a citation you can open.


Open source models
What you can download and run yourself, and how far behind it is.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Afternoon
text:
The other eighty per cent


Yesterday
Rows, columns, joins. Five spreadsheets and a total you could reconcile.

Everything else a firm holds
Contracts, mail, board papers, policies, reports, decks, notes.


65% of data leaders call their structured data ready for AI. 39% say the same of the unstructured kind, which is most of the volume.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Afternoon
section: Why not just paste it in
text:
Why not just paste it in


It was not trained on yours
Your contracts were not on the public web. Nothing in the weights knows them.


The window is finite
A million tokens is large and your document store is larger.


You pay for every turn
Input is billed each turn. Pasting the corpus into every question bills the corpus every question.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Afternoon
text:
Four steps


Chunk. Split the documents into passages of a few hundred words.
Embed. Turn each passage into a vector, the same way tokens became vectors on Thursday.
Retrieve. Embed the question and find the handful of passages closest to it.
Paste. Put those passages in the prompt, with the question.



The model never reads your corpus. It reads an excerpt that a similarity search chose.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Afternoon
text:
A passage becomes 384 numbers

An embedding model reads a passage and returns a fixed-length list of numbers — 384, or 768, or 1,536, depending on the model.

Passages about the same thing land near each other, whatever words they used. “Revenue fell in the third quarter” sits close to “Q3 sales were down”, and a keyword search for “revenue” finds only the first.

This is why retrieval works on a question phrased in the reader’s words rather than the author’s.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Afternoon
text:
Chunking is the design decision







Choice
What it costs




Chunks too small
the passage arrives without the sentence that made it mean something


Chunks too large
the relevant line is buried in a page of irrelevance you paid for


Split mid-table
numbers arrive with no column headings


No overlap
an answer spanning a boundary is never retrieved whole



Split on the document’s own structure — sections, clauses, slides — before falling back on a word count.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Afternoon
text:
Two ways to have one


A hosted tool
Upload the folder, ask questions. Somebody else chose the chunking, the embedder and the number of passages retrieved.

A pipeline you own
Your chunking rules, your embedder, your store, and the retrieved text visible before it reaches the model.

Start hosted. Build your own when the answers are wrong and you need to see which passages came back.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Afternoon
section: Build one over your own documents
text:
Build one over your own documents
Exercise 16 · 60 minutes


Put twenty or more of your own documents in a folder — reports, policies, decks, anything real but not confidential.
Have them chunked and embedded into a local store, and have the chunking rule stated in writing.
Add a search tool to an agent, so it retrieves before it answers.
Ask five questions you already know the answers to.
Make it print the passages it retrieved, not just the answer.



Step 5 is the whole exercise. An answer you cannot trace is the thing RAG was supposed to fix.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Afternoon
section: Make it cite, then check the citation
text:
Make it cite, then check the citation

A citation is only worth having if somebody opens it.



Ask a question whose answer is in exactly one document.
Ask one whose answer is spread over three.
Ask one whose answer is in none of them, and see whether it says so.



The third is the one that fails. A retriever always returns its closest matches, whether or not any of them are relevant.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Afternoon
text:
Permissions do not survive chunking


The document
Sat in a folder with an access list. Three people could open it.

The chunk in the store
Is a row in a database with a vector next to it. Usually carries no access list at all.

Index everything and the retriever will hand a new analyst a paragraph from a file they could never have opened.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Afternoon
text:
Retrieved text is untrusted text

A poisoned document in the index is a prompt injection with a delivery mechanism.

Anything that reaches the model reaches it as text, and text from a retrieved passage arrives in the same stream as your question. Whoever can put a document into the index can put instructions in front of the model.

Which is the Sunday morning question again: who can write to the corpus, and what can the agent do once it has read one.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Afternoon
section: When it is the wrong tool
text:
When it is the wrong tool


Few enough to paste
Twenty pages fit in the window. Retrieval adds a failure mode and buys nothing.


The answer is a number
Totals, counts and rankings come from a query against the data, not a similarity search over prose.


The corpus changes hourly
Every change means re-embedding. A live query beats a stale index.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Afternoon
text:
Break your own
Exercise 17 · 40 minutes


Add a document to your index that contradicts another one. Ask the question both answer.
Add one containing an instruction addressed to the agent. Ask an unrelated question.
Ask something answered only by a table you chunked in the middle.
Write down which of the three your setup handled, and what you would change.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Afternoon
text:
Screen shares

What you indexed, and how you chunked it
One question it answered well, with the passage it used
The one that broke it

title: Saturday, September 26 · Afternoon
text:
What GPQA Diamond measures

Four-way multiple-choice questions in biology, physics and chemistry, written by people who hold or are working toward a PhD in the field they wrote for.



25% guessing


34% skilled non-experts, 30+ minutes of open web search


74% PhDs answering inside their own field



Diamond is the hardest 198 of the 448 questions: both expert annotators answered correctly and most non-experts did not. Rein et al., 2023.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Afternoon
text:
How far behind is it?


Each line is that tier’s best score so far; gray dots are every other model. Source: Epoch AI, 8 Sep 2026.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Afternoon
text:
What Terminal-Bench measures

An agent is given a container, a plain-English objective, and a terminal. It has to actually do the job: compile the code, train the model, configure the server, find the bug.



7 task domains: software, ML, science, operations, security, hardware, media


4 parts to a task: instruction, container, test suite, reference solution


0 or 1 per task — the tests pass or they do not



Built by the Laude Institute with Stanford researchers. No human baseline is published. The version charted here dates from mid-2025; a harder v4.0 has since cut the frontier to about 60%.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Afternoon
section: The same three tiers, on agentic work
text:
The same three tiers, on agentic work


Epoch’s mirror of Terminal-Bench; its closed-model coverage runs to April 2026.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Afternoon
text: Where each tier stands today

title: Saturday, September 26 · Afternoon
text:
Two numbers, two different answers


The months
Three to five months, on both benchmarks. A model small enough for one consumer GPU is nine to ten months back, on both.

The scores
On graduate science questions the open gap is 3 points. On agentic terminal work it is 33, and the small model solves 23% against the frontier’s 85%.

GPQA Diamond is near its ceiling, which compresses the gap: five months of lag is worth three points because there is nowhere left to go. Terminal-Bench is not near any ceiling, and there the same few months is most of the task.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Afternoon
section: What that means for a choice
text:
What that means for a choice


Answer from knowledge
A 27B open model scores 86% on GPQA Diamond against the frontier’s 96%, on hardware you own.


Reason over your documents
A large open model is a few months behind and self-hostable. Test it on your own task before taking the ranking.


Run a multi-step agent
On Terminal-Bench the best open model solves 52% and the best small one 23%, against the frontier’s 85%.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Afternoon
section: Not every job needs the largest model
text:
Not every job needs the largest model









Where it runs
What it suits




A frontier model
the provider’s API
judgment, long context, code


A mid-size model
the same API, less per token
classification, extraction, routing


A small open model
your own hardware
high volume, or data that cannot leave


A fine-tuned small model
your own hardware
one narrow task, done constantly



On a single question the price difference is negligible. On a million classifications it is the budget.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Afternoon
text:
Distillation, in one paragraph

Run the frontier model on a few thousand examples of your task. Keep the inputs and its outputs. Train a small model on those pairs.

The small model does not become generally capable. It becomes capable at the one task you sampled, at a fraction of the cost per call, on hardware you control.

title: Saturday, September 26 · Afternoon
text:
Tomorrow
Everything so far has run inside a tool somebody else built. Tomorrow you go under it, and then ask what it would take to let one loose on real data.
